---
title: "Making Requests: The Request Queue Workflow"
description: "Why asynchronous requests to your supervisor go through a request queue instead of email or Slack, and how the workflow works in practice."
categories: [Policies, Communication]
---

## The problem this solves

Most research groups run coordination through email and chat: a student sends a message, the
supervisor reads it whenever they next check their inbox, and from that point the request lives
as an open loop in both people's heads until it's resolved. Cal Newport calls this the
**hyperactive hive mind** workflow in *A World Without Email* — work gets accomplished through
an ongoing stream of ad hoc, unscheduled messages, with no defined process for how a request
moves from "sent" to "done." Every message demands a decision: read it now or lose track of it,
reply now or potentially lose track of it later.

Two costs follow from this. First, **attention residue**: switching from focused work to answer
a message doesn't just cost the minute it takes to reply. Attention lingers on the interrupted
task, and again on the message, for a while after the switch, which is part of why "I'll just
answer this quickly" so reliably costs more than a quick moment. Second, **underspecified
requests generate their own overhead**. A message like "can you take a look at my draft?"
looks fast to send, but if it doesn't say what kind of look, by when, or against what standard,
it turns into a back-and-forth negotiation before any actual work happens. This back-and-forth
competes for the same inbox attention as everything else.

None of this is a complaint about email as a technology. It's a description of what happens by
default when a channel designed for quick, synchronous-feeling exchanges is used to route actual
work.

## The reverse task list

*Slow Productivity*, also by Newport, describes an alternative: a **reverse task list**. Instead
of a system where anyone can add something to your plate at any moment simply by sending a
message (a *push* system), a reverse task list is a *pull* system. Requests accumulate in a
queue that the recipient reviews and pulls from on their own schedule, rather than being
forced into their attention in real time.

The request queue applies that idea directly, built around three rules:

1. **The requester bears the burden of specifying the request clearly.** This saves the recipient
   from having to deal with vague requests for which additional information needs to be requested.
   Each of these exchanges costs time and leads to delays.
2. **Submitting a request does not mean it has been accepted.** Larger requests ("Long Actions")
   go into a review queue and are explicitly accepted or declined, rather than silently becoming
   an obligation the moment they're sent.
3. **Once accepted, you can see the status yourself.** No follow-up email needed to ask "did you
   see this?" or "where is this in the queue?"

## How it works

Requests go in through a public submission form at
[tasks.chrisdegroot.ca](https://tasks.chrisdegroot.ca). There's no login for requesters. Each
submission gets a private tracking link instead (more on that below).

**Every request is classified at submission time.** The form asks one question: could this
reasonably be completed in about 10 minutes once your supervisor opens it, including reading any
linked material?

- **Quick Actions** (yes) go straight into a queue and get worked through in a batch session,
  in order of urgency and then age.
- **Long Actions** (no) go to a review queue first. Your supervisor either **accepts** it (it
  joins an ordered queue of accepted work), **declines** it with a reason, or asks a clarifying
  question before deciding.

**Requests are supposed to be self-contained.** The form asks for a clear description of the
action needed, any relevant links, and whatever context is needed to act on it without further 
discussion. There's a checkbox confirming you believe everything needed is there. This friction 
is deliberate: it's the mechanism that enforces rule 1 above. Writing the request out completely 
up front is almost always faster overall than an underspecified request bouncing back and forth 
over several exchanges.

**If something's missing, the request comes back to you, not into a conversation.** Rather than
your supervisor guessing or messaging you to ask, the request moves to a "Needs Information"
state with a specific question attached. You get notified, answer it through your tracking link,
and the request resumes automatically (right back into the queue near where it left off, not at
the end).

**You track status through a private link, so you don't need to ask about it.** Submitting (or 
being asked for information) gives you a tracking URL. You should save it, so you can refer back
later. That page shows the request's current status, its position in the queue if it's an accepted 
Long Action, and its full history. You'll also get pinged automatically by email when your request 
is received, accepted, declined, needs more information, or completed. In practice you shouldn't 
need to check the link proactively very often, since you will get these email updates, but provides
a means to check on the status in between. 

## What this isn't for

The request queue is specifically for asynchronous, well-defined work requests. It is not a
replacement for every kind of communication with your supervisor.

- **Not for scheduling meetings.** If you need to actually talk something through, use the
  meeting booking link on the submission page instead. The whole point of the queue is to handle
  requests that *don't* need a live conversation.
- **Not for quick clarifying chats.** If a request is genuinely just a quick question with an
  answer that doesn't require any real work, the queue adds overhead rather than removing it —
  ask directly instead.
- **Not a general project-management tool.** It doesn't replace your OKRs (see
  [Tracking Student Progress with OKRs](../project-management/student-okrs.qmd)) or a shared task 
  board for ongoing work. It's for one-off requests directed at your supervisor specifically: 
  reviewing something, approving something, making a decision, signing something.

## Further reading

- Cal Newport, *Slow Productivity* — the reverse task list / pull-based workflow this system is
  built around.
- Cal Newport, *A World Without Email* — the hyperactive hive mind workflow problem, and why
  process-driven alternatives beat ad hoc messaging for anything beyond a quick exchange.
- Cal Newport, *Deep Work* — attention residue, and why context-switching costs more than it
  appears to in the moment.
